[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance describes how a Platform Engineering author produces a Golden Path infrastructure module that conforms to [PTN-INFRA-GOV-003](../../../../patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-003-golden-path-infrastructure-module-pattern.md). PTN-INFRA-GOV-003 is the normative specification — it defines the three mandatory provision categories, the four required module outputs, and the IaC plan OPA checks that every conforming module must satisfy. This guidance covers the authoring sequence, the decisions an author must make before writing any IaC code, the staging validation required before outputs can be delivered to dependent component authors, and the pre-submission verification required before scheduling architecture review.

This guidance is technology-profile-agnostic: the three provision categories — Workload Isolation Boundary, Workload Identity, and Resource Attribution — apply to every Golden Path regardless of workload runtime (Kubernetes, ECS, Lambda, MFE/CDN, Batch). The specific IaC resource types, inspection commands, and identity binding mechanisms are technology-profile-specific; where they appear in this guidance they are presented as examples with the platform profile labeled, not as normative requirements. See GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001 Approach 2 and the technology profile notes in PTN-INFRA-GOV-003 for platform-specific implementation detail.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- An infrastructure module authored to this guidance satisfies PTN-INFRA-GOV-003 by construction  Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture review is performed at the catalog level once, not per ARB submission cycle
- The four required outputs (`namespace_name`, `workload_identity_ref`, `secrets_store_uri`, `isolation_enforcement_level`) are populated with real values from a staging apply before any dependent component author begins work — placeholder values in workload identity artifacts become a pre-delivery failure, not a silent production incident
- Terraform plan OPA checks defined in the Verification Contract pass on every plan evaluation because the module is pre-validated before publication  teams do not discover infrastructure misconfiguration at service instantiation time

#### Scope Boundaries

- **In Scope**: Authoring the three mandatory provision categories, declaring the four required module outputs, and satisfying the Terraform plan OPA checks defined in the path's Verification Contract

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#business-context]

### Business Context

The infrastructure module is the dependency root of the Golden Path bundle. The security template author cannot finalize the workload identity artifact until the cloud provider identity resource exists and its reference is output by the module. The scaffold author cannot configure the secrets integration artifact until the secrets store URI is output. A Golden Path bundle cannot be submitted to the ARB until the infrastructure module outputs are populated with real, validated values from a staging environment.

This sequencing dependency has a direct consequence: the infrastructure module must be authored and validated against a staging environment before any other component author can finalize their path constants. The coordination point is Phase 6 of this guidance  delivering the four required outputs to the security template author and scaffold author. Teams that skip this step and use placeholder values are the primary source of silent workload identity authentication failures in production. The workload starts; the secrets operator fails to authenticate; secrets are never synced. There is no crash, no error at apply time  only a running pod with no secrets.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

- **Regulatory workload volume**: HIPAA-scoped and ARC-AMPE co-scoped workloads are growing; each requires infrastructure-layer NIST 800-53 r5 control evidence. A catalog-level infrastructure module produces that evidence structurally via OPA checks  not per-service, per-assertion.
- **Platform Engineering scale**: Platform Engineering cannot individually review every service's infrastructure configuration. A catalog-level module reviewed once is inherited by all services on the path without individual re-review.
- **Production incidents from incomplete modules**: Silent workload identity authentication failures caused by placeholder credential references or incorrectly scoped identity bindings are the most frequent production incident category for regulated-scope services.
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#strategic-alignment]

#### Strategic Alignment

This guidance implements the [Enterprise Golden Path Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/enterprise-golden-path-strategy.md) requirement that Golden Path infrastructure modules deliver pre-wired security configurations as path constants, not as consumer choices. It directly supports the Zero Trust Architecture mandate (NIST SP 800-207): ZTA Tenet 3 (per-workload scoped identity) and Tenet 6 (dynamically verified access) are enforced structurally at the infrastructure layer — teams cannot bypass them because the infrastructure module, not the service team, provisions the identity and access policy.

This guidance also implements the [Enterprise Architecture Verification Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/enterprise-architecture-verification-strategy.md) requirement that verification is a concurrent design obligation, not a post-build addition. The infrastructure module author is responsible for all four verification layers: Layer 1 (module root file presence), Layer 2 (post-apply fitness functions), Layer 3 (co-defined policy-as-code assertions), and Layer 4 (tagging and naming design for runtime drift detection). A Golden Path is not complete until its verification suite is complete; for the infrastructure module, that means all four layers are satisfied.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

Golden Path infrastructure modules are stored at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/` in the Golden Path Catalog repository. They are standard Terraform child modules invoked by the CI/CD pipeline at the infrastructure provisioning stage of a path's deployment sequence. Module inputs are split into two categories per PTN-INFRA-GOV-003:

- **Consumer inputs** (`service_name`, `team`, `environment`): Supplied by the consuming team or CI/CD pipeline at instantiation time. Non-security-bearing.
- **Path constants**: All security-bearing values (isolation enforcement level, identity resource naming convention, identity binding scope pattern, least-privilege access scope, required tag set) are encoded as `locals` in `main.tf`. They are not consumer-overridable.

Infrastructure module correctness is verified across the four layers defined in the [Enterprise Architecture Verification Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/enterprise-architecture-verification-strategy.md) and operationalized per path through PTN-GOV-AI-003 (Verification Contract). The infrastructure module author has design and execution obligations at each layer:

- **Layer 1 — Structural Conformance Gate** (build time): Verifies that `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, and `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` are present at `catalog/infrastructure/{path-id}/`. This gate runs automatically at the start of every CI/CD pipeline execution and blocks all downstream stages on failure. The author's obligation is to confirm these four files are present and correctly named locally before pushing — file presence does not verify content correctness, but file absence blocks the entire pipeline immediately.

- **Layer 2 — Fitness Functions** (pipeline stage gates): Executable tests for architectural properties that cannot be evaluated from file structure or IaC plan JSON alone. For the infrastructure module, the Layer 2 fitness functions are the post-apply behavioral validation steps in Phase 6: isolation enforcement baseline validation (using the platform-appropriate inspection command to confirm the enforcement configuration is active on the provisioned boundary resource) and the end-to-end workload identity chain test (deploying a test execution context using the provisioned `workload_identity_ref` value and confirming secrets store authentication succeeds). These tests verify that the architectural decisions encoded in the provision categories are correctly implemented and functional in a real environment — not just structurally present in the plan. The author is responsible for authoring, running, and recording the output of both fitness functions before declaring outputs deliverable.

- **Layer 3 — Policy-as-Code** (pre-deployment gate): OPA/Rego policies evaluate `terraform show -json` plan output before `terraform apply` runs. The Terraform plan checks defined in the path's Verification Contract assert that all three provision categories are correctly configured. This is a veto gate — a check failure blocks `terraform apply`. The infrastructure module author **co-defines** the Layer 3 check assertions for their provision categories with the Verification Contract author (GUID-GOV-IMPL-001). The infrastructure author has the deepest knowledge of the Terraform plan JSON shape for each resource type — the field paths, resource type names, and assertion values. Check assertions authored without this input are frequently wrong in their Rego JSON path expressions and fail at Phase 7 requiring multi-phase re-work.

- **Layer 4 — Runtime Monitors** (post-deployment, continuous): AWS Config, Azure Policy, or GCP Config rules compare deployed resource state against declared Terraform state on a continuous basis. Drift triggers an automated incident. The infrastructure module author's obligation at Layer 4 is **design**: the four required tags (`compliance_scope`, `path_id`, `environment`, `team`) and the identity resource naming convention that includes `path_id` are the labels by which the runtime monitoring layer identifies which resources belong to which path and detects drift. A module that applies tags inconsistently or uses a naming convention that omits `path_id` produces resources the runtime monitor cannot attribute to a path — drift against declared state goes undetected.

The number and specific assertions of the Layer 3 Terraform plan checks are defined per path in the Verification Contract — they are not a fixed universal set. This guidance refers to them as "the TF checks defined in the Verification Contract" and uses check ID notation (e.g., TF-001) only in examples.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#current-state-assessment]

#### Current State Assessment

- Target platform environments (Kubernetes clusters, ECS clusters, Lambda environments, CDN distributions) provide platform-level workload identity prerequisites — these are platform-layer prereqs; the Golden Path infrastructure module builds on them.
- OPA/Rego policy evaluation (`opa eval`) is available in platform CI/CD agents; the policy bundle for each path is maintained in the Verification Contract.
- No standardized authoring workflow exists — multiple Golden Path submissions have reached ARB with incomplete or incorrectly scoped modules, requiring rework.
- Provider versions in existing catalog modules vary; some are unpinned, producing upgrade drift between development and CI/CD environments.

#### Future State Vision

- Every Golden Path infrastructure module authored to this guidance passes the Verification Contract TF checks on first ARB submission.
- The four required outputs (`namespace_name`, `workload_identity_ref`, `secrets_store_uri`, `isolation_enforcement_level`) function as a stable interface contract — downstream component authors consume them by name regardless of which technology profile or path they are working with.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Without authoring guidance, infrastructure modules are produced with the most visible resources present but the critical integration details missing: an isolation boundary without the enforcement baseline configuration encoded as a path constant; an identity resource without a binding scoped to the correct workload execution context; a secrets access policy scoped to a wildcard account or subscription rather than the specific secrets resource. These gaps do not produce errors at apply time — they produce workloads that start but fail silently. The modules appear complete from a resource presence perspective; the plan structure is valid; the OPA checks fail only because the path-specific assertions (enforcement baseline value, binding scope format, resource scope) are not met.

The ARB then reviews a module that cannot integrate with the security template and scaffold as designed, requiring a rework cycle before any component author can proceed with real output values.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#principle-1-read-the-verification-contract-before-writing-any-hcl]

#### Principle 1: Read the Verification Contract Before Writing Any HCL

**Description:** The Terraform plan checks defined in the path's Verification Contract are the specification. No HCL resource block should be authored before the assertions those checks encode are understood in plain English.

**Rationale:** The most common source of OPA check failure at Phase 7 is a Terraform resource authored against memory or convention rather than against the specific assertion. Label key exact-match checks and trust policy subject regex checks in particular fail with no visible HCL error  the resource exists, the plan succeeds, but the assertion fails. Authoring against the check assertions before writing code closes this gap.

**Application:** Complete Phase 1 (Verification Contract review and policy bundle smoke-test) in full before creating any `.tf` file. For each check in the bundle, write its assertion in plain English and keep it visible while authoring the resource it validates.
page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#principle-2-infrastructure-outputs-before-dependent-component-authoring]

#### Principle 2: Infrastructure Outputs Before Dependent Component Authoring

**Description:** The infrastructure module must be applied to a staging environment and its four required outputs captured before the security template or scaffold authoring phases begin.

**Rationale:** The workload identity annotation value and secrets store URL embedded in downstream artifacts are path constants  they cannot be placeholders. A `terraform plan` output does not produce these values; only `terraform apply` against a real environment resolves the cloud provider resource references. An empty string delivered as `workload_identity_ref` passes structural OPA checks (annotation key presence) and reaches production silently.

**Application:** Complete Phase 6 (staging apply and output delivery) before signalling to the security template author that GUID-SEC-IMPL-001 Phase 1 can begin. Gate downstream authoring on receipt of `infra-outputs-staging.json`, not on completion of the Terraform plan.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#principle-3-security-bearing-values-are-path-constants-not-consumer-inputs]

#### Principle 3: Security-Bearing Values Are Path Constants, Not Consumer Inputs

**Description:** Every value with security implications — isolation enforcement level, identity resource naming convention, identity binding subject pattern, secrets access scope — is a path constant encoded as a `local` in `main.tf`. It is not a `variable` with a default that a consumer can override.

**Rationale:** A `variable` with a default can be overridden at apply time using `-var` or a `.tfvars` file. A `local` cannot. A team that can override the isolation enforcement level or supply their own secrets access scope has effectively disabled the infrastructure-layer controls the module is supposed to enforce structurally.

**Application:** Before authoring each resource, identify every field with security implications. Encode those as `locals`. Consumer inputs are limited to `service_name`, `team`, and `environment`. Mark every path constant with a code comment: `# Path constant  not a consumer input`.
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#principle-4-validate-per-phase-not-at-the-end]

#### Principle 4: Validate Per Phase, Not at the End

**Description:** Run the OPA checks relevant to each provision category immediately after authoring that category  not as a batch at Phase 7.

**Rationale:** A batch validation at Phase 7 across a three-phase authoring process produces multiple concurrent failures across different resource types. Each failure must be traced back to the resource that caused it, which requires re-reading several provision categories at once. Validating per phase surfaces each failure in context, while the relevant code is still on screen and the check assertion is the current focus.

**Application:** After each provision category (Workload Isolation Boundary, Workload Identity, Resource Attribution), run the subset of checks that validate it, confirm they pass, and then proceed. Run the full suite at Phase 7 as confirmation only.
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#principle-5-architecture-review-before-arb-not-during]

#### Principle 5: Architecture Review Before ARB, Not During

**Description:** Infrastructure Architecture sign-off must be obtained before the ARB submission package is assembled  not during the ARB session.

**Rationale:** The ARB confirms that the bundle is complete and that the correct reviewers have already signed off. It does not perform technical infrastructure review. Infrastructure Architecture validates the provision category design, identity scope, and compliance tagging. Security Architecture validates the trust policy binding and secrets access scope. Both reviews must complete before ARB.

**Application:** Schedule Infrastructure Architecture and Security Architecture co-review at Phase 7, after the full OPA suite passes. Do not submit to ARB without both written sign-offs in the package.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#approach-1-check-driven-resource-authoring]

#### Approach 1: Check-Driven Resource Authoring

**Overview:** For each provision category, read the Verification Contract check assertions first, translate them into plain-English resource requirements, then author the minimum IaC code that satisfies each assertion.

**When to Use:** All new Golden Path infrastructure modules. Ensures all Verification Contract checks are satisfied by construction rather than discovered as failures during full-suite validation.

**Steps:**
1. Obtain the Verification Contract check YAML files from GUID-GOV-IMPL-001 Phase 4
2. For each check, write the assertion in plain English (example: "the Workload Isolation Boundary resource must have an enforcement baseline configuration set to the path-constant value for the path's compliance scope")
3. Author the minimum IaC resource that satisfies the assertion
4. Run `opa eval` against `terraform show -json` immediately after each resource block — do not proceed to the next resource until the relevant check passes

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#approach-2-adapt-from-a-validated-existing-module]

#### Approach 2: Adapt From a Validated Existing Module

**Overview:** When the new path's infrastructure requirements closely match an existing catalog path, adapt the existing module rather than authoring from scratch.

**When to Use:** When the new path shares the same compliance scope, technology profile, and secrets access pattern as an existing path with a validated module.

**Steps:**
1. Copy the validated module from `catalog/infrastructure/{existing-path-id}/`
2. Update `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` with the new `path_id` and the new Verification Contract check ID references
3. Update the identity resource name `local` to reference the new `path_id`
4. Confirm the identity binding subject or trust condition matches the new path's workload execution context naming convention
5. Run the new path's full Verification Contract check suite against the adapted module's plan

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

- **Apply to staging before delivering any output.** `terraform plan` does not create resources. Cloud provider identity resource references are only resolved after `terraform apply`. A plan-time `terraform output` for a new resource returns an empty string. Delivering an empty `workload_identity_ref` unblocks downstream authors with an invalid value that passes structural checks and fails at runtime.
- **Pin all provider versions explicitly.** Unpinned provider references can silently adopt a new provider version on `terraform init`, breaking plan schema compatibility. Use `~>` constraints pinned to the minor version. Confirm the enterprise-approved version range with the Platform Infrastructure team before authoring.
- **Document path constants with their engineering rationale.** A future author who sees a least-privilege secrets access scope without context may escalate it to a broader scope for perceived reliability. A code comment explaining that the scope satisfies the least-privilege check and the workload's only required access prevents this escalation pattern.
- **Confirm the workload execution context identifier with the scaffold author before authoring the identity binding.** The identity binding subject format varies by technology profile (see Technology Profile Reference — Table 2) and must exactly match the execution context created by the scaffold. Read the scaffold template directly — do not rely on verbal confirmation.
- **Fill `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` before writing any `.tf` file.** The manifest forces explicit decisions about isolation enforcement level, compliance scope, required tag set, and TF check IDs before any implementation begins. Decisions at the manifest level are stable; decisions implied by IaC code are frequently revised to pass a check rather than encoding the organizationally correct value.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- **Isolation enforcement baseline absent or on wrong resource type.** The enforcement baseline configuration must be applied to the Workload Isolation Boundary resource for the target technology profile (see Technology Profile Reference — Table 1 for the correct resource type and enforcement configuration). Most platforms silently ignore security configuration on object types that do not support them — there is no error, but the isolation boundary has no enforcement in place. After apply, validate using the platform-appropriate inspection command (see Technology Profile Reference — Table 3).
- **Identity binding subject does not match the workload execution context.** A binding for the wrong service account name, task role, or execution role principal causes a silent identity token exchange rejection. The pod or task starts; the secrets mechanism cannot authenticate; secrets are never synced. This is the highest-frequency production failure for HIPAA-scoped workloads. Confirm the exact execution context identifier with the scaffold author before authoring the binding.
- **Secrets access scope too broad.** A secrets access policy scoped to a wildcard account, subscription, or resource group grants the workload identity access to secrets it has no business accessing. The Verification Contract's least-privilege check will catch this. Scope must be the specific secrets resource (secret ARN or Key Vault resource ID).
- **Dependency ordering: identity binding authoring before isolation boundary exists in state.** If the binding interpolates from the isolation boundary resource before it has been applied, Terraform produces a dependency error. Use a `local` for the boundary name that matches the resource's `name` field by construction, avoiding the runtime dependency.
- **Provider version unpinned.** An unpinned provider on `terraform init` can upgrade silently, breaking plan schema compatibility. Pin providers explicitly; confirm approved version ranges with Platform Infrastructure.
- **Sensitive output override.** Adding `sensitive = false` to `workload_identity_ref` or `secrets_store_uri` outputs to avoid masked log values will cause the output sensitivity check to fail. Use masked pipeline variables to manage log visibility — do not remove the sensitivity declaration.
- **Delivering outputs from Terraform plan rather than apply.** After plan, new resources have no resolved cloud provider references. `terraform output` after plan returns placeholder or empty values for resources that do not yet exist. The staging apply is required before outputs can be delivered.

        - Confirm the Rego path expression resolves in the smoke-test against a minimal synthetic plan JSON
        The infrastructure author, not the Verification Contract author, knows the terraform show -json
        plan shape for each resource type. Assertions must be agreed before IaC authoring begins.

     Confirm platform prerequisites with Platform Engineering:
        - Platform-level workload identity federation mechanism active for the target technology profile

        - Secrets store address (ARN, URI, or resource ID) for the target environment confirmed
        - Cloud provider identity naming convention approved by Security Architecture
        - Isolation enforcement level approved for the path's compliance scope

Phase 2: Module Root and Manifest

      (provision categories, TF check IDs, required outputs, compliance scope, isolation enforcement level)
     Create variables.tf: three consumer inputs + path constants with # Path constant comments
     Confirm: no security-bearing value is exposed as a consumer variable

Phase 3: Workload Isolation Boundary

        - Isolation enforcement baseline configuration set to path-constant value
          (resource type and enforcement configuration per Technology Profile Reference — Table 1)
        - path_id, compliance_scope, environment attribution labels/tags
        - required tags from locals.required_tags
     Run OPA checks for Workload Isolation Boundary provision category
     All isolation-boundary-related checks must return true before proceeding

        (identity resource type, binding subject format, and access policy scope per

     Identity binding subject/condition must match the workload execution context created by scaffold;
        confirm the exact subject format against Technology Profile Reference — Table 2 and the

     Run OPA checks for Workload Identity provision category
     All identity-related checks must return true before proceeding

Phase 5: Resource Attribution and Output Declarations
     Add locals.required_tags block; apply to all cloud provider and platform resources
     Author outputs.tf:
        namespace_name            (not sensitive)
        workload_identity_ref     (sensitive = true)  # identity resource reference per platform
        secrets_store_uri         (sensitive = true)  # secrets store address per platform

#### Decision Point 1: Per Service or Per Path-Environment Provisioning?

**Context:** The module provisions a namespace and a cloud provider identity resource. Should it be invoked once per path-environment pair (all services on the path share the namespace and identity), or once per service instance?

**Options:**
- Per path-environment: One namespace, one identity resource per environment. Services are differentiated by service account name within the shared namespace.
- Per service instance: A new namespace and identity resource provisioned for every service instantiation.

**Recommendation:** Per path-environment for most paths. Per-service provisioning creates a proliferation of identity resources per environment and complicates network policy management. Per-service isolation is a pattern variation requiring a Platform Engineering architecture review  not a consumer input override.

#### Decision Point 3: Identity Binding Subject — Per Workload Execution Context or Wildcard?

**Context:** The identity binding (trust policy condition, federated credential subject, or task role assignment) binds the cloud provider identity to a specific workload execution context. A wildcard would allow any execution context in the isolation boundary to exchange tokens.

**Recommendation:** Always per workload execution context — the exact binding subject format for each technology profile is in Technology Profile Reference — Table 2. A wildcard binding means any workload in the isolation boundary can use the identity, violating ZTA Tenet 3. The Verification Contract's trust binding check asserts the subject is not a wildcard; a wildcard will fail this check.

#### CSF 1: Verification Contract Checks Co-Defined and In Hand Before Authoring

The Verification Contract check YAML files must be present and the policy bundle must load successfully before any HCL resource block is authored. But receipt of files is not sufficient — the infrastructure author must actively co-define the Layer 3 check assertions with the Verification Contract author. The infrastructure author knows the Terraform plan JSON shape; the Verification Contract author knows Rego. Both inputs are required for assertions that are both syntactically correct Rego and semantically aligned with what the HCL will produce.

If the Verification Contract author has not yet produced the check YAML files, Phase 1 is not complete. Do not begin Phase 2 by estimating what the checks will assert.

Phase 1 is complete when: the policy bundle loads without parse errors, each check's assertion is documented in plain English with the agreed Terraform resource type and JSON field path, and the Rego path expressions have been confirmed in the smoke-test against a minimal synthetic plan JSON.

#### Case Study 1: Trust Binding Naming Mismatch

**Background:** An initial EKS infrastructure module was authored and applied to staging. All Verification Contract checks passed. After the first service deployment, the secrets operator reported a failed secret sync with no further detail.

**Root cause:** The scaffold author confirmed workload execution context naming verbally as `{service_name}`. The scaffold template actually creates execution contexts as `{service_name}-svc`. The OIDC trust policy condition referenced `{service_name}`. AWS STS rejected the token exchange silently.

**Resolution:** OIDC trust policy condition updated to match `{service_name}-svc`. Module re-applied. `infra-outputs-staging.json` re-confirmed. Workload identity chain test succeeded.

**Lesson encoded:** Read the scaffold template directly in Phase 1. Verbal confirmation is not sufficient. This is now Critical Success Factor 3 in this guidance. The Verification Contract trust binding check validates pattern structure; it does not validate the name against the scaffold template — that cross-validation is the author's responsibility.

#### Case Study 2: Compliance Scope Extension  Version Discipline

**Background:** Twelve services were running on a path at v1.0.0 (HIPAA only) when CMS Medicaid requirements mandated ARC-AMPE compliance for Medicaid-processing workloads.

**Approach:** `compliance_scope` updated to include ARC-AMPE; `arc_ampe_scope: "true"` tag added; Verification Contract updated with new ARC-AMPE tag assertion check. Version bumped from `1.0.0` to `2.0.0`  the `required_tags` change is a breaking plan diff for every existing deployment.

**Migration:** v1.0.0 remained active while teams migrated to v2.0.0 via the adoption playbook. No emergency rollout required. All twelve teams migrated within two sprint cycles.

**Lesson:** Compliance scope changes are always major version bumps. The pre-submission checklist covered v2.0.0 without modification  the checklist is compliance-scope-agnostic because it checks for the presence of required tags, not their values.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#implementation-lessons]

#### Implementation Lessons

- **Confirm the workload execution context naming by reading the scaffold template directly in Phase 1.** A mismatch discovered post-Phase 4 requires deleting and recreating the identity binding resource and may require a staging environment reset.
- **Run the OPA policy bundle smoke-test before Phase 3.** Discovering incorrect Rego JSON path expressions at Phase 7 causes multi-phase re-work. A Phase 1 smoke-test against a minimal synthetic plan JSON confirms path expressions before authoring begins.
- **Apply to staging before delivering any output.** There is no exception. Placeholder or empty outputs in downstream artifacts produce workloads that start and fail silently.
- **Book both architect sign-offs as a joint session.** Sequential scheduling adds an average of five business days to the review timeline.

[strategy/guidance/infrastructure/implementation/GUID-INFRA-IMPL-001-golden-path-infrastructure-module-authoring-guidance.md#best-practices-discovered]

#### Best Practices Discovered

- **Encode all path constants as `locals` in `main.tf`, not as `variable` defaults.** A `variable` with a `default` can be overridden with `-var`. A `local` cannot.
- **Include `isolation_enforcement_level` as a module output even if consuming components rarely use it directly.** The compliance metadata author requires it. Omitting it requires a module patch after publication.
- **Verify the secrets store exists in the target environment before Phase 6.** Discovering it does not exist at Phase 6 adds a full provisioning day. Confirm its address alongside the platform-level identity prerequisites in Phase 1.
- **Compliance scope changes are always major version bumps.** Any change to `compliance_scope` or `required_tags` is a breaking plan diff for every existing deployment using the module.

### Risk Management

| Risk | Description | Probability | Impact | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Identity binding mismatch | Identity binding subject does not match the workload execution context created by scaffold; identity auth fails silently at secrets sync time | High | High | Confirm execution context identifier by reading scaffold template directly in Phase 1; identity binding TF check verifies pattern format but not name-against-scaffold |
| Outputs delivered from plan, not apply | Outputs delivered as empty values; downstream authors embed empty references | Medium | High | Phase 6 requires `terraform apply` before output delivery; pre-submission checklist confirms staging apply completed |
| Secrets access scope too broad | Policy scoped to wildcard account, subscription, or resource group rather than specific secrets resource | Medium | High | Secrets scope TF check; secrets access scope is a path constant, not a consumer input |
| Isolation enforcement baseline absent or on wrong resource | Isolation boundary created without enforcement configuration | Low | High | Isolation enforcement baseline TF check; validate using platform-appropriate inspection command after apply |
| Provider version drift | Unpinned provider upgrades silently and breaks plan schema | Low | Medium | Pin all providers explicitly; confirm approved version ranges with Platform Infrastructure |
| Sensitive output override | `sensitive = false` override exposes credential reference in CI pipeline logs | Low | Medium | Output sensitivity TF check; use masked pipeline variables instead |
| Compliance scope not declared before authoring | Isolation enforcement level or tag set revised to pass a check rather than encoding the correct value | Medium | Medium | Fill `infrastructure-module-manifest.yaml` in Phase 2 before any IaC code is written |
